title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
full_review:
Playing a dual role as hero and villain, comic actor Mike Myers portrays a leftover Swinging Sixties single, ``Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery'' (Gramercy).

As written by Myers and directed by Jay Roach, this is a fairly lame spoof of the James Bond 007 movies, opening in 1967 when gaudy, big-toothed secret agent Austin Powers is inexplicably a magnet to all the young women in swinging London. The opening musical number is actually quite zippy and a colorful send-up of the mod look of the era as plastic-booted, miniskirted women pursue their idol.

However, when Powers' nemesis, the villainous Dr. Evil (Myers), chooses to be cryogenically frozen to continue his misdeeds in the future, Powers does likewise.

Presto -- it's 1997 -- Dr. Evil reanimates with Powers in his wake and once again they must face off lest the dastardly doctor activate all the earth's volcanoes simultaneously.

 

That's about it as far as plotting goes with most of the time lavished on -- some would argue wasted on -- Myers' boorish, leering Powers, who is assigned a female partner (Elizabeth Hurley) he expects to bed as easily as in the good old days.

The movie is simply a vanity piece for Myers' brand of tasteless toilet humor and sexual innuendo, in a series of drawn-out skits better suited to late-night TV shows.

But for movie addicts there are the inside joke references to previous films that add a little much-needed fun to the mix because the one-joke premise of both characters being behind the times wears thin pretty darn quickly.

In fact, Powers' ubiquitous crushed velvet suits have more life in them than some of the worn-out sight gags that are trotted out and stretched to death.

 

Clearly in the flick just for the paycheck are Robert Wagner, Michael York, Carrie Fisher and Mimi Rogers in roles you would miss if you blinked.

Myers' fans may enjoy his mocking of all things British, but the movie is hard-pressed to sustain a comic sensibility even for its modest 87 minutes.

Due to a fleeting sexual encounter, some comically intended violence, much crude humor and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Catholic Conference classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
